title: A boundary on paper
bodyMd:
A dialect map may draw a crisp boundary between two pronunciations, yet the interviews underlying it often reveal gradual change. Speakers in neighbouring villages may use both forms, selecting one with relatives and another at work. A mapmaker must nevertheless choose a rule for assigning each village to a region. One rule counts the most frequent form; another records any use of the supposedly local form. Applied to the same interviews, these rules can produce different boundaries.

The resulting disagreement need not mean that either map is carelessly made. A boundary is a summary of a distribution, and different summaries serve different purposes. What becomes misleading is presenting the summary as though speakers themselves obeyed a sharp geographic division. A useful map should therefore make its classification rule visible and, where possible, indicate mixed usage rather than hide it.
